Trial.Public_title: Effect of cerebral electrical stimulation combined with physical exercise on pain reduction and functional improvement in individuals with knee osteoarthritis
Trial.Scientific_title: Effect of Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation combined with Lower Limb Muscle Strengthening Exercises on pain and functionality in patients with knee Osteoarthritis: a randomized controlled trial
Trial.Study_design: a phase n/a, randomized-controlled, double-blind, parallel, treatment
Trial.Contact_Address: Avenida Jovino Fernandes Sales, 2600, bairro Santa Clara
Trial.Contact_Affiliation: Universidade Federal de Alfenas
Trial.Inclusion_Criteria: Inclusion criteria: Male and female participants; age between 50 and 75 years; symptomatic knee osteoarthritis for at least 3 months; pain score greater than 3 on the 0–10 Numeric Rating Scale (NRS); Kellgren–Lawrence classification greater than grade 1
Trial.Exclusion_Criteria: Exclusion criteria: History of cancer; patients with type I diabetes; with uncontrolled arterial hypertension; with cardiac pacemaker; presenting neurological deficits; with orthopedic surgery in the lower limbs; with body mass index above 40 kg/m²; with symptomatic hip osteoarthritis; presenting cognitive impairment; with history of brain surgery; seizure; stroke or intracranial metal implantation; who underwent craniectomy at the site of transcranial direct current stimulation application; and decompensated ventricular shunt
Trial.Intervention: This is a two-arm, double-blind, randomized controlled clinical trial. Participant randomization will follow a table of random numbers generated using the electronic tool Research Randomizer. Experimental group: Fifteen participants will receive transcranial direct current stimulation combined with lower limb strengthening exercises. Control group: Fifteen participants will receive sham transcranial direct current stimulation combined with the same lower limb strengthening exercises. For the transcranial direct current stimulation intervention, the Microestim transcranial direct current stimulation device (NKL, Brusque – SC, Brazil, ANVISA 80191680008) will be used. The stimulation parameters will include a constant current intensity of 2 mA, 30-second ramp-up and ramp-down periods, and sponge electrodes moistened with 0.9% saline solution to reduce impedance and enhance current penetration. Each transcranial direct current stimulation session will last 20 minutes. The electrode placement will follow the 10–20 system: the anodal electrode will be positioned over the primary motor cortex contralateral to the affected knee, and the cathodal electrode will be placed over the supraorbital area ipsilateral to the affected knee. Sham stimulation will mimic the appearance and sensation of active transcranial direct current stimulation but will deliver the 2 mA current for only 30 seconds. Both the experimental and control groups will perform lower limb strengthening exercises. A total of 10 sessions will be conducted over two consecutive weeks, excluding Saturdays and Sundays. Each session will last approximately 40 minutes, structured as follows:The first 20 minutes will involve the simultaneous application of transcranial direct current stimulation and a 10-minute warm-up on;E02.331.800;G11.427.410.698.277
Trial.Primary_outcome: A variation in pain intensity is expected, measured by the Numerical Rating Scale (0 to 10), with a significant reduction in pain levels anticipated between pre- and post-intervention assessments
Trial.Secondary_outcome: A decrease in functional limitation is expected, measured by the Lequesne Index (0 to 24 points), with a significant reduction in functional limitation levels anticipated between pre- and post-intervention assessments;An improvement in functional mobility is expected, assessed by the Timed Up and Go (TUG) test, considering that shorter execution times indicate better performance. A significant reduction in test completion time is anticipated when comparing pre- and post-intervention measurements;A decrease in the physical activity score (0 to 68) is expected, measured using the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index (WOMAC), when comparing pre- and post-intervention results, considering that higher scores indicate lower levels of physical activity;An increase in muscle strength of the knee extensors and flexors is expected, assessed using a handheld dynamometer, when comparing pre- and post-intervention values, considering that higher values indicate improved muscle strength;An improvement in postural balance is expected, assessed using the Biodex Balance System (BBS), when comparing pre- and post-intervention values, considering that lower sway values indicate better postural control

Trial.Public_title: Optimizing therapeutic exercise for shoulder overuse syndrome: effects on edema reduction, range of motion, and pain relief using data-driven approaches
Trial.Scientific_title: Effects of exercise therapy on pain reduction, range of motion, and pectoralis minor muscle length in elderly patients with shoulder pain: A randomized controlled trial comparing exercise therapy to a placebo intervention
Trial.Study_design: Single-blind parallel-group randomized controlled trial (Treatment, Efficacy)
Trial.Inclusion_Criteria:
Inclusion criteria: 1. Age: Participants aged 60 years or older.
2. Chronic Shoulder Pain: Participants with chronic shoulder pain lasting at least 3 months.
3. Diagnosis: Participants with a diagnosis of shoulder impingement syndrome, rotator cuff tendinopathy, or other musculoskeletal disorders causing shoulder pain.
4. Range of Motion: Participants with limited shoulder range of motion (abduction or external rotation).
5. Pain Level: Participants with a Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain score of at least 4 (moderate pain) at baseline.
Trial.Exclusion_Criteria:
Exclusion criteria: 1. Acute Shoulder Injury: Participants with recent shoulder injuries (less than 3 months) or acute trauma to the shoulder.
2. Surgical History: Participants who have had shoulder surgery in the past 6 months.
3. Severe Shoulder Dysfunction: Participants with severe loss of shoulder function or contraindications to physical activity.
4. Other Medical Conditions: Participants with neurological, cardiovascular, or musculoskeletal conditions that affect the shoulder or prevent participation in the intervention.
5. Pregnancy: Female participants who are pregnant or planning to become pregnant during the study period.
6. Uncontrolled Health Conditions: Participants with uncontrolled diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, or any other systemic illness that could interfere with participation.
7. Non-compliance: Participants who are unable or unwilling to comply with the study protocol or follow-up visits.
Trial.Condition:
Chronic shoulder pain in elderly patients
Musculoskeletal Diseases
Trial.Intervention:
This study is a single-blind, parallel-group, randomized controlled trial (RCT) conducted at a tertiary care rehabilitation center. Randomization was achieved using a computer-generated sequence, with block randomization (block size of 4) to ensure balanced allocation between two groups. Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to one of two intervention arms:

Exercise Therapy (ET): A structured program involving stretching and strengthening exercises aimed at improving shoulder mobility, reducing pain, and enhancing muscle length. The program includes exercises targeting the scapular stabilization and shoulder strengthening.

Physiotherapy (Placebo): A control intervention consisting of standard physiotherapy modalities including infrared therapy, ultrasound therapy, and transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), with no active therapeutic benefit to the shoulder's functional capacity.

Both groups received their allocated intervention for 18 sessions across the 6-week period, with all sessions supervised. There were no changes to the trial design after commencement, and the study followed the pre-defined methods throughout.

Outcomes were assessed at baseline and post-intervention (immediately after the 6-week program). The single-blind aspect refers to the outcome assessment, where the evaluator measuring outcomes was blinded to group allocation. Participants were also unaware of the existence of the other treatment arm to minimize bias.
Trial.Primary_outcome: Pain reduction as measured by the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for shoulder pain intensity at baseline and post-intervention (immediately after the 6-week program)
Trial.Secondary_outcome:
The secondary outcome measures were assessed at baseline and post-intervention (immediately after the 6-week program):
1. Range of Motion (ROM): Improvement in shoulder abduction and external rotation range of motion, measured using a goniometer
2. Pectoralis Minor Muscle Length: Changes in the pectoralis minor muscle length, measured using ultrasound or muscle length measurement techniques
Trial.results_ipd_description:
Stored in publicly available repository. This study is committed to making the individual participant data (IPD) available to the research community to promote transparency and allow for further analysis.
1. Data Storage and Repository: The datasets generated during this study will be stored in a publicly available repository such as: Open Science Framework (OSF) or Zenodo, ensuring the data is accessible to researchers globally. Link to be provided after study publication.
2. Type of Data to be Shared: The following data will be shared: Demographic information (age, gender, etc.) Pain scores (measured by the Visual Analog Scale, VAS) Range of motion measurements (abduction and external rotation) Pectoralis minor muscle length measurements (using ultrasound)
3. Data Availability Timeline: The IPD will be made publicly available 12 months after the study’s publication. The data will be stored in a publicly accessible repository (OSF/Zenodo), and links to the data will be shared in the publication's supplementary materials.
4. Access Criteria: The data will be available to researchers upon request for non-commercial academic research purposes only. Requests for data will be submitted via a formal contact (e.g., study PI or designated team member) and will require a research proposal that meets ethical and scientific criteria. Contact for Data Requests: Dr Bhishma Karki, bhishma.karki@trc.tu.edu.np
5. Mechanism of Data Sharing: Data will be shared via a secure online repository (e.g., OSF or Zenodo) where datasets will be anonymized and made available through a public link. Data will be made available with appropriate anonymization to ensure participant confidentiality and comply with GDPR or relevant data protection laws.
6. Consent from Participants: Informed consent was obtained from all study participants prior to enrollment. The consent forms include clauses about the use of anonymized data for research purposes.
7. Ethical and Legal Restrictions: Ethical approval was obtained from the Ethics Committee of Tribhuvan University (Kathmandu, Nepal). The shared data will be anonymized and will not include any personally identifiable information (PII). Data will not be shared with any commercial entities unless participants' explicit consent is obtained.
8. Comments on Data Anonymization: All shared data will be fully anonymized by removing participant identifiers such as names, addresses, or any direct identifiers. Only aggregated, de-identified data will be available to ensure that participants' privacy is maintained.
9. Exceptions: In case of unforeseen circumstances or legal restrictions (e.g., specific local laws or data protection issues), access to data may be restricted, but we will provide a clear rationale for any such limitations.
10. Long-term Availability: The dataset will remain accessible for at least 5 years after the publication date, allowing researchers to explore the data for further studies or meta-analyses.

Trial.Public_title: Effects of Neck Treatment and Exercise on Spine Alignment
Trial.Scientific_title: The Effects of Cervical Manipulation and Isometric Neck Exercise on Segmental Spinal Alignment Angles: A Retrospective Study
Trial.Study_design: Observational Study Model : Cohort, Time Perspective : Retrospective, Enrollment : 230, Biospecimen Retention : Collect & Archive- Sample without DNA, Biospecimen Description : Not Applicable
Trial.Contact_Address: 3F/4F, 49-9 Samseong-dong, Samsung Balance Clinic, Gangnam-gu, Seoul, Korea
Trial.Contact_Affiliation: Samsung Balance Clinic
Trial.Inclusion_Criteria:
Inclusion criteria: 1.Patients who received cervical manipulation and isometric neck exercises at ?? Clinic in Seoul within the study period
2.Adults aged between 20 and 60 years
3.Patients with a cervical lordotic angle (C1–C7 Cobb’s angle) of less than 35°, verified by lateral cervical radiography
4.Patients for whom complete lateral cervical, lumbar, and sacral radiographic data were available pre- and post-intervention.
Trial.Exclusion_Criteria:
Exclusion criteria: 1.History of trauma, fracture, or surgery in the cervical spine region
2.Conditions including spinal tumors, infectious diseases, ankylosing spondylitis, congenital spinal deformities, or severe degenerative changes hindering radiographic angle measurements
3.Poor quality of radiographic imaging, hindering accurate measurement
4.Incomplete radiographic data (cervical, lumbar, sacral) either pre- or post-intervention
5.History of similar spinal treatment at other medical institutions.
Trial.Condition: ;Diseases of the musculoskeletal system and connective tissue
Trial.Primary_outcome: Changes in Cervical Lordotic Angle (C1–C7 Cobb’s angle)
Trial.Secondary_outcome: Changes in Lumbar Lordotic Angle (L1–S1 Cobb’s angle)
Trial.results_summary: This retrospective study analyzed changes in spinal sagittal alignment angles and their inter-segmental correlations following an 8-week intervention consisting of cervical manipulation and isometric neck exercises (4 weeks each) in 130 patients with cervical hypolordosis. After intervention, cervical lordotic angle increased significantly from 28.27° to 31.69° (mean increase of 3.42°, p<0.001), lumbar lordotic angle improved from 43.59° to 44.71° (mean increase of 1.12°, p=0.009), and sacral slope rose from 34.39° to 35.54° (mean increase of 1.15°, p<0.001). Multiple regression analysis showed a significant correlation between lumbar lordotic angle and sacral slope changes (p<0.001), whereas changes in cervical lordosis were not significantly correlated with lower spinal segments. The results indicate cervical manipulation and isometric neck exercises are effective in improving spinal alignment in patients with cervical hypolordosis, suggesting spinal alignment is regulated through complex, multidimensional mechanisms.

Trial.Public_title: Effect of 8-week of Jiu-jitsu exercise program on body composition, physical fitness, autonomic nervous system function, and mental health parameters in adolescents
Trial.Scientific_title: Effect of 8-week of Jiu-jitsu exercise program on body composition, physical fitness, autonomic nervous system function, and mental health parameters in adolescents
Trial.Study_design: Primary Purpose : Other(Reviewing the effects of 8 weeks of jiu-Jitsu exercise on the body composition, physical fitness factors, autonomic nervous system function, and mental health indicators of adolescents), Intervention Model : Parallel, Blinding/Masking : Open, Allocation : RCT
Trial.Contact_Affiliation: Konkuk University
Trial.Inclusion_Criteria:
Inclusion criteria: A person who has agreed to participate in this study and voluntarily agreed to the written consent
Adolescents aged 13 to 19 living in S city (ages 12 to 18)
Adolescents who have not performed any special exercise and have no experience in jiu-jitsu exercise
Trial.Exclusion_Criteria:
Exclusion criteria: Persons aged 13 to 19 (ages 12 to 18) who are not eligible for adolescence
A person who has a clinical condition (e.g., cardiovascular disease, respiratory disease, musculoskeletal disease, etc.) that is difficult to perform the jiu-jitsu exercise program
A person who has participated in a regular exercise program within six months
Other researchers deemed unfit to participate in this study
A person who has not obtained the consent of his/her legal representative (parent)
Trial.Condition: ;Factors influencing health status and contact with health services
Trial.Intervention:
Behavioral : The control group should maintain the same daily life as usual for 8 weeks.
The experimental group performs a jiu-jitsu exercise program equivalent to the level of RPE 6 to 10 for 50 to 70 minutes per day three times a week for 8 weeks.
Trial.Primary_outcome: Body composition (height, weight, fat mass, body fat mass, body fat mass, body fat percentage, waist circumference, and hip circumference);Physical factors (strength, muscle endurance, flexibility, cardiopulmonary endurance, agility, quickness, balance);Mental health indicators (stress, general anxiety disorder, depression)
Trial.Secondary_outcome: heart rate variability
Trial.results_summary: The effects of the 8-week jiu-jitsu exercise program on adolescents' physical composition, physical fitness factors, autonomic nervous system function, and mental health indicators were as follows. In the case of body composition, the amount of fat increased significantly in both the control group and the experimental group (CON: 0.7kg vs EXP: 0.77kg), and the body fat percentage increased significantly in the control group but decreased significantly in the experimental group (CON: 0.45% vs EXP: -0.67%). In the case of physical fitness factors, significant interaction effects were found in the grip strength (p=0.015, ? p2=0.287), the left forearm (p<0.001, ? p2=0.511), and the eye-opening external footwear (p=0.035, ? p2=0.224), the back muscle strength (p<0.001, ? p2=0.481), the sit-up (p=0.032, ? p2=0.230), the 15m shuttle run (p<0.001, ? p2=0.626), and the in-place long jump (p=0.002, ? p2=0.415). In the case of autonomic nervous system function, SDNN (p=0.009) and RMSSD (p=0.018) were significantly increased in HRV, and LF (p=0.023) was significantly decreased, improving autonomic nervous system function. In the case of mental health indicators, there was no difference between GAD-7 and BDI, but PSS (p=0.001, ? p2=0.455) showed a significant interaction effect, and PSS decreased by 5.9 points, which significantly reduced stress. Putting these results together, it was confirmed that the 8-week treatment of the jiu-jitsu exercise program for adolescents aged 12 to 18 is effective in improving body composition (body fat rate), physical factors (strength, muscle endurance, cardiopulmonary endurance, flexibility, quickness, equilibrium), autonomic nervous system function (SDNN, RMSSD, LF, HF, LF/HF), and mental health indicators (PSS). In the future, additional controlled studies are needed for adolescents with low mental health indicators, including more sample size, longer-term interventions, daily activity and dietary intake surveys, and indicators that can explain clear physiological mechanisms.

Trial.Contact_Affiliation: Konkuk University
Trial.Inclusion_Criteria:
Inclusion criteria: - consent to participate in this study and signed by the written consent of this study
- It is corresponding to 19 and 29 years old and registered in Korea University Sports Council
- A person who participated in sports activities ( baseball)
Trial.Exclusion_Criteria:
Exclusion criteria: - a special disease or injury within six months
- A sports unique stress that provides sports unique stress and muscle exercise provided in this study
- Now, there's a self-defense that has a shoulder surgery experience of shoulder surgery, and neurological diseases
- A person who has currently injuries such as waist disk or wrist joint
- a person who judged that the foreign researcher was inappropriate
Trial.Intervention:
Others(strength exercises, stretching) : Twenty-four subjects were classified into 12 control groups (CON) that maintain their daily lives through equal division and 12 exercise groups (EXE) that consist of sports-specific stretching and strength exercises. Then, the subjects in the CON maintained their normal daily life for six weeks, and the subjects in the EXE performed a 50-minute exercise program consisting of warm-up, stretching, strength training, and clean-up exercises for six weeks, three times a week.
In this study, the sports-specific stretching and strength training programs performed by the subjects belonging to the EXE group consist of warm-up, stretching, strength training, and clean-up exercises. Warm-up exercises were conducted for 10 minutes with intensity corresponding to 4 to 5 based on the Borg scale of exercise (RPE). Stretching consisted of eight movements (biceps brachii stretch, pronator muscle stretch, triceps muscle stretch, rhomboid stretch, sleeper stretch, cat cow, pelvic stretch, spin mobility) and was conducted for 10 minutes at an intensity corresponding to RPE 2 to 3. The strength training consisted of four movements (YTWL w/band, push-up plus w/band, plank w/band, and single leg reaching) and was conducted for 20 minutes at an intensity corresponding to RPE 7 to 8. Finally, the warm-up exercise was performed for 10 minutes at an intensity corresponding to RPE 2. This sports-specific stretching and strength training program was conducted for EXE for 6 weeks, 3 times a week, for 50 minutes per session. On the other hand, subjects belonging to the CON group were instructed to maintain their daily lives as mentioned above.
Trial.Primary_outcome: pitching velocity;muscle stiffness;range of motion;functional movement screen
Trial.Secondary_outcome: body composition
Trial.results_summary:
1. In the case of body composition, there were no changes due to sports-specific shoulder, spine, pelvic stretching and muscle strength training treatment for 6 weeks. Through this, it was confirmed that the other dependent variables reviewed in this study, such as muscle stiffness, range of motion, functional movement screen, and pitch speed, were not affected by body composition.
2. In terms of muscle stiffness, the six-week sports-specific shoulder, spine, pelvic stretching, and muscle strength training treatment significantly reduced the muscle stiffness of the serratus anterior, and in the exercise group, the muscle stiffness of the subscapsular muscle decreased significantly, but the muscle stiffness of the serratus anterior, gluteus maximus, and hip rotator muscles increased significantly. Based on this, it was confirmed that the six-week exercise treatment applied in this study acts to increase flexibility by lowering the stiffness of the shoulder muscles, and to increase muscle activity by increasing the stiffness of the arm and pelvic muscles.
3. In terms of joint motion range, sports-specific shoulder, spine, pelvic stretching, and strength training for 6 weeks significantly reduced the range of motion for extra-shoulder rotation, pelvic flexion, and extra-pelvic rotation in the control group, and significantly increased the range of motion for all 9 movements in the exercise group. These results confirmed that the exercise treatment applied in this study effectively improved the range of motion for the shoulder, spine, and pelvis.
4. Functional movement evaluation, a functional movement screen that shows a high correlation with physical function and baseball performance, showed significant improvement by sports-specific shoulder, spine, pelvic stretching, and muscle exercise treatment for 6 weeks in the exercise group.
5. In the case of restraint, which is the pitch speed, a significant improvement effect was found by sports-specific shoulder, spine, pelvic stretching, and muscle exercise treatment for 6 weeks in the exercise group.
6. In the correlation between pitch speed, muscle stiffness, range of motion, and functional movement screen, pitch speed showed a significant inverse correlation with muscle stiffness of the subscapular and light muscles, and significant positive correlation was shown with hip rotator muscle stiffness, intra-shoulder rotation, extra-shoulder rotation, pelvic flexion, pelvic distortion, joint range of motion in extra-pelvic rotation, and functional movement evaluation.

Trial.Public_title: How a low-carbohydrate diet affects blood sugar and health in people living with type 2 diabetes: results from a real-life study
Trial.Scientific_title: The lifestyle club feasibility study
Trial.Contact_Address: 21PGM00, The Leggett Building, University of Surrey
Trial.Inclusion_Criteria:
Inclusion criteria: 1. Over 18 years age
2. Diagnosis of type 2 diabetes as defined by an HbA1c over 47mmol/mol
Trial.Exclusion_Criteria:
Exclusion criteria: 1. Pregnant or planning pregnancy in the ensuing 12 months
2. Active treatment for cancer or terminal illness
3. Kidney disease or renal stones
4. Proliferative retinopathy
5. Recovering from acute surgery
6. Gout
7. Gallbladder disease
8. Pancreatic disease
Trial.Intervention:
An 8-week online dietary and lifestyle program, to facilitate a low-carbohydrate diet (LCD)

The intervention was a health coaching service delivered by The Lifestyle Club (TLC), part of the Public Health Collaboration, a UK-registered charity (Charity no. 1171887/SC052248). Patients were directed by their surgery to a booking website to register for an information session delivered via Zoom or Microsoft Teams. Multiple sessions were offered at different times (morning, afternoon, evening). A health coach led each session, explaining the course and low-carbohydrate approach. Registrants received an email with a course enrolment form to collect contact, medical, medication details, and consent. After enrolling, participants were sent confirmation emails with their coach’s name, session details, and access link. The 8-session course covered topics including T2D, LCDs, shopping tips, understanding food labels, eating out, and intermittent fasting. Coaches used discovery learning to assess participants' prior knowledge and foster group interaction to overcome challenges. The GRIN model for behaviour change was incorporated, encouraging participants to set goals, reflect on resources, plan Incremental changes, and notice progress in health aspects such as energy, sleep, mood, and weight. A WhatsApp group was created for participants to connect, ask questions, and share progress. After the course, participants were invited to monthly catch-up sessions, Facebook and WhatsApp communities, and local TLC peer support groups. Participants were advised to follow an LCD, but without a specific target of carbohydrate g/day. No specific restrictions were placed on fat intake, provided that it was derived from whole, unprocessed foods, rather than artificial or processed foods. Foods
Trial.Primary_outcome:
1. Serum cholesterol measured using standard laboratory procedures at an accredited NHS laboratory (Berkshire and Surrey Pathology Service, at The Royal Surrey Hospital) at baseline, 3 months and 6 months
2. Weight measured using a Tanita weighing scale at baseline, 3 months and 6 months
3. Waist circumference measured using a tape measure at baseline, 3 months and 6 months
4. Body fat and lean body mass measured using bioimpedance at baseline, 3 months and 6 months
5. Food frequency measured using a questionnaire evaluated through interviews at baseline and 6 months
Trial.Secondary_outcome:
1. Glucose-lowering medication usage for type 2 diabetes measured using recall at baseline and 6-months
2. Blood HbA1c measured using standard laboratory procedures at an accredited NHS laboratory (Berkshire and Surrey Pathology Service, at The Royal Surrey Hospital) at baseline, 3 months and 6 months
Trial.results_ipd_description: Available on request. The datasets generated during and/or analysed during the current study are/will be available upon request from Dr.Martin Whyte, 21PG00 Leggett Building, University of Surrey, Guildford, UK. Email: m.b.whyte@surrey.ac.uk. Data will be in batched, anonymised form and available for up to 10 years after completion of the study.

Trial.Public_title: How do individuals with HIV feel when performing Intense Exercise?
Trial.Scientific_title: Acute effect of High-Intensity Interval Training on immunological parameters, cardiac autonomic control and psychophysiological responses of people living with HIV: a randomized clinical trial
Trial.Primary_sponsor: Departamento de Educação Física da Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte - Lagoa Nova Campus Central
Trial.Study_design: a phase n/a, randomized-controlled, single-blind, cross-over, treatment
Trial.Contact_Affiliation: Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte
Trial.Inclusion_Criteria: Inclusion criteria: men with HIV; between 18 and 45 years of age; who have been on ART for at least 6 months; medical authorization to practice physical exercise; physically active for at least 1 month
Trial.Exclusion_Criteria: Exclusion criteria: Individuals with any musculoskeletal limitation that prevents exercise; history of cardiovascular disease; use of illicit drugs; smokers; alcoholics; those who did not follow the evaluation recommendations
Trial.Intervention: This study is a randomized, crossover clinical trial. The sample and population consisted of 50 physically active male participants with and without HIV, aged 18 to 40 years. One session of each exercise model was performed and assessed before, during, and at the end of the session. Participants completed all three sessions in random order. The HIIE-HV consisted of 4x4 minutes at 80% of Wmax, the HIIE-LV consisted of 10x60 seconds at 90% of Wmax, and the MICE was performed at 60% of Wmax for 30 minutes. Psychophysiological markers (pleasure, affect, perceived exertion, and intention to exercise) were assessed;G11.427.410.698.277.311.250
Trial.Primary_outcome: Expected outcome 1: To assess and compare the acute psychological responses of people living with HIV (PLWH) and healthy individuals following a single session of three different exercise protocols: low-volume high-intensity interval exercise (HIIE-LV), high-volume high-intensity interval exercise (HIIE-HV), and moderate-intensity continuous exercise (MICE). The psychological variables include: affective responses (Feeling Scale, from -5 to +5), perceived pleasure (7-point scale), and future intention to engage in exercise (0–100% scale). Assessments will be conducted before, during, and after each exercise session;Outcome found 1: A significant difference between groups was found only for the “pleasure” variable following the HIIE-HV protocol, with higher scores observed in the PLWH group (p = 0.031), indicating a more positive psychological response to this type of exercise. No significant differences were found between groups for affective responses or future exercise intention (FEI). During exercise, a time effect (p < 0.001) and a time × condition interaction (p = 0.003) were observed for affective responses, indicating increased affect over time in both groups. In the control group, HIIE-HV elicited significantly lower affective responses at specific time points compared to HIIE-LV and MICE. These findings suggest that healthy individuals may perceive differences in exercise intensities more distinctly than PLWH
Trial.Secondary_outcome: Expected outcome 2: To compare ratings of perceived exertion (RPE) across the different exercise protocols (HIIE-LV, HIIE-HV, and MICE) throughout the sessions in both groups (PLWH and healthy controls). It is expected that, despite differences in RPE between protocols, affective responses will be similar among exercise types for PLWH, which may indicate greater tolerance and potential adherence to high-intensity interval training;Outcome found 2: Significant effects of time (p < 0.001), exercise method (p = 0.041), and time × method interaction (p < 0.001) were observed for RPE. In the PLWH group, the HIIE-HV protocol elicited significantly higher RPE scores across almost all stages when compared to HIIE-LV and MICE. Similar patterns were observed in the control group. Despite this, affective responses did not differ significantly between exercise methods within the PLWH group, supporting the hypothesis of possible tolerance and acceptability of high-intensity interval exercise among these individuals
Trial.Source_Support: Departamento de Educação Física da Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte - Lagoa Nova Campus Central;Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte - Lagoa Nova Campus Central
Trial.Secondary_Sponsor: Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte - Lagoa Nova Campus Central
Trial.results_summary: Pleasure was significantly higher in PLWH after HIIE-HV (p = 0.031), while RPE was also higher during HIIE-HV in both groups. No significant differences in affect or future exercise intention were observed between groups. Control participants showed lower affective responses during HIIE-HV, while PLWH maintained similar affective responses across all exercise types. These results suggest that HIIE protocols, particularly HIIE-HV, may be well tolerated and positively received by PLWH.
Trial.results_baseline_char: A total of 22 participants were included, with 11 people living with HIV (PLWH) and 11 healthy controls. The groups were similar in age (PLWH: 34.4 ± 5.54 years; Controls: 33.3 ± 5.92 years), BMI (PLWH: 25.8 ± 3.43; Controls: 26.7 ± 3.09), and VO2max (PLWH: 33.3 ± 6.20 ml/min/kg; Controls: 35.9 ± 6.28 ml/min/kg). All PLWH had undetectable viral load and were on antiretroviral therapy (ART) for an average of 6.2 ± 3.1 years. Most used a combination of NRTI + II.
Trial.results_adverse_events: No adverse events were reported during or after any of the exercise sessions. All participants tolerated the protocols well.
Trial.results_outcome_measures: Primary outcomes included psychological responses (affect, pleasure, and future exercise intention) measured before, during, and after each exercise session. Secondary outcomes included perceived exertion (RPE), oxygen consumption (VO2), average watts, heart rate, and caloric expenditure during exercise

Trial.Public_title: Effectiveness of Auriculotherapy on fatigue, sleep and quality of life in nursing students: study with data collection before and after the intervention
Trial.Scientific_title: Effectiveness of Auriculotherapy on fatigue, quality of life, and sleep of nursing university students: quasi-experimental study
Trial.Study_design: a phase n/a, single-arm-study, single-blind, other, treatment
Trial.Contact_Affiliation: Universidade Federal de Santa Maria
Trial.Inclusion_Criteria: Inclusion criteria: Students from the 4th semester to the 8th semester regularly in the nursing course and who have not had total or partial suspension of the course; students who obtain scores of poor sleep quality and high fatigue; all genders and over 18 years old
Trial.Exclusion_Criteria: Exclusion criteria: Students who are partially or completely suspended from the course will be excluded from the intervention if they are undertaking other energetic therapies (Reiki, therapeutic touch, yoga, Ayurveda, among others); use of anxiolytics; antidepressants and pregnant women
Trial.Condition: fatigue; Disorders of excessive somnolence; Quality of life;F02.830.855.734.500
Trial.Intervention: This is a quasi-experimental study, without a control group, which assesses participants before and after the intervention. Participant selection: Before starting the intervention, validated instruments will be administered to identify: high fatigue (Fatigue Assessment Scale - FAS) and poor sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index - PSQI). Only students who present high scores on these items will be invited to participate in the intervention. Thus, the intervention sample will be 40 students. Auriculotherapy is based on Traditional Chinese Medicine and uses the ear as a reflex map of the human body. Specific points are stimulated with seeds, needles, or metal spheres, usually fixed with micropore. The intervention will be applied once a week for 6 consecutive weeks, each session lasting an average of 15 to 20 minutes. The sessions will be conducted by a trained professional (the researcher herself has completed training in the area). At each session, the auricular points will be cleaned, stimulated with seeds or spheres, fixed, and self-care guidance provided (massaging the points throughout the week). Students will be monitored via WhatsApp messages, and reactions, complaints, and symptom progression will be recorded during the sessions. To ensure traceability of the intervention, participants will receive self-care instructions and will be able to report any changes they notice between sessions. In the first, third, sixth, and final six weeks, the same instruments used at the beginning will be reapplied to measure the technique's effectiveness in the following areas: fatigue, sleep, drowsiness, and quality of life.;E02.190.204
Trial.Primary_outcome: Auriculotherapy to reduce fatigue and improve the quality of sleep of university nursing students.
Trial.Secondary_outcome: Auriculotherapy to improve the quality of life of university nursing students
Trial.Source_Support: Universidade Federal de Santa Maria;Programa de Pós-Graduação em Enfermagem da Universidade Federal de Santa Maria
Trial.Secondary_Sponsor: Programa de Pós-Graduação em Enfermagem da Universidade Federal de Santa Maria

Trial.Public_title: Effects of Time-Restricted Eating on Body Weight and Physical Performance in Young Adults
Trial.Scientific_title: ime-Restricted Eating Without Exercise Enhances Anaerobic Power and Reduces Body Weight: A Randomized Crossover Trial in Untrained Adults - TRE-APW Trial
Trial.Contact_Address: C201, Haruha Lane, 7247-1 Jike, Saijo-cho, Higashihiroshima-shi, Hiroshima 739-0041, Japan
Trial.Contact_Affiliation: Graduate School of Humanities and Social Sciences, Hiroshima University Department of Educational Sciences
Trial.Inclusion_Criteria: Inclusion criteria:
Trial.Exclusion_Criteria: Exclusion criteria: - Individuals with a diagnosed history of cardiovascular, metabolic, or musculoskeletal disorders - Individuals who currently smoke or consume alcohol on a regular basis - Individuals who are actively participating in a structured exercise program during the study period (e.g., sports club activities, personal training) - Individuals who are unable or unwilling to comply with the time-restricted eating schedule or dietary control - Individuals engaged in shift work or those with irregular sleep-wake cycles - Individuals participating in other clinical trials during the study period - Individuals who are unable to provide written informed consent
Trial.Intervention:
Early Time-Restricted Eating (eTRE): Participants were instructed to consume all meals within a 6-hour window between 08:00 and 14:00 each day, and to refrain from any caloric intake outside this window. The intervention lasted for 4 weeks, and no exercise intervention was implemented. Primary outcomes included changes in body weight, aerobic endurance, and anaerobic power.
Delayed Time-Restricted Eating (dTRE): Participants were instructed to consume all meals within a 6-hour window from 12:00 to 18:00 each day, and to refrain from any caloric intake outside this window. The intervention lasted for 4 weeks, with no exercise intervention. Primary outcomes included changes in body weight, aerobic endurance, and anaerobic power.
Trial.Primary_outcome: Change in body weight (measured at baseline, 4 weeks, and 10 weeks after intervention initiation)
Trial.Secondary_outcome: AAerobic endurance: time to exhaustion on a cycle ergometer at a constant workload of 150 W for men and 90 W for women, defined as the point when cadence could no longer be maintained at >=60 rpm for 10 consecutive seconds (measured at baseline, 4 weeks, and 10 weeks after intervention initiation); Anaerobic power: peak power output during three 10-second maximal cycling sprints on a cycle ergometer (measured at baseline, 4 weeks, and 10 weeks after intervention initiation)
Trial.results_baseline_char: A total of 28 healthy university students (12 males and 16 females, aged 18-26 years) participated in this study. All participants had a body mass index (BMI) below 30 and no history of cardiovascular, metabolic, or musculoskeletal disorders. None of the participants were engaged in any structured exercise program during the study period.
Trial.results_outcome_measures: The study included the following three primary outcome measures: Body weight: Measured in the afternoon (between 15:00 and 17:00) at each assessment point (baseline, week 4, and week 10), under standardized fasting conditions. Aerobic endurance (time to exhaustion): Assessed using a cycle ergometer at constant load (150 W for men, 90 W for women). The test ended when cadence fell below 60 rpm for more than 10 consecutive seconds. Anaerobic power (peak power output): Participants performed three 10-second all-out sprints on a cycle ergometer, and the highest peak power output (in watts) was recorded. All outcomes were assessed at baseline, after 4 weeks, and after 10 weeks of intervention.

Trial.Scientific_title: Impact of Silk Nightcap Use on Hair Manageability, Sleep Quality, and Psychological Well-being: A Crossover Randomized Comparative Study - Impact of Silk Nightcap Use on Hair Manageability, Sleep Quality, and Psychological Well-being: A Crossover Randomized Comparative Study

Trial.Inclusion_Criteria: Inclusion criteria:
Trial.Exclusion_Criteria: Exclusion criteria: Exclusion criteria for study participation are as follows: 1) Individuals who decline to participate of their own will 2) Individuals judged to be ineligible by the principal investigator 3) Individuals who routinely use a silk nightcap

Trial.Primary_outcome: To evaluate changes in morning hair combing ease resulting from the use of a silk nightcap using a five-point Likert scale.

Trial.Public_title: Chakra aromatherapy for nurses
Trial.Scientific_title: Chakra-based aromatherapy reduces stress and improves sleep in nurses: a randomized controlled trial
Trial.Inclusion_Criteria:
Inclusion criteria: 1. Registered nurses working in hospital settings
2.Willing to participate and provide written informed consent
Trial.Exclusion_Criteria:
Exclusion criteria: 1. Atopic dermatitis
2. Respiratory disease
3. Pregnancy or lactation
Trial.Condition:
Quality of life of nursing staff
Other
Trial.Intervention:
After participants signed the consent form, random numbers were drawn based on gender, with odd-numbered participants assigned to the experimental group and even-numbered participants assigned to the control group (41 participants each). The random sequence was generated and maintained by an assistant not involved in recruitment and intervention to ensure that allocation was concealed and minimize bias.

82 nurses were randomly divided into an experimental group and a control group, with 41 people in each group. The treatment lasted 30 minutes five times a week for four consecutive weeks.

Chakra-based aromatherapy:
Participants will receive chakra-based aromatherapy using essential oils applied with inhalation and massage, 30 minutes per session, 5 times per week, for 4 weeks.

Routine care:
Participants will continue with routine care and will not receive aromatherapy intervention. The control group was given a placebo.
Trial.Primary_outcome: Sleep quality measured by the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) at baseline and 4 weeks

Trial.Public_title: Comparing sprint-interval training and moderate intensity continuous exercise training for fitness improvements in healthy females
Trial.Scientific_title: Peak oxygen uptake response to twelve weeks of sprint-interval or moderate-intensity continuous training in healthy females: A randomized non-inferiority trial
Trial.Study_design: Single-centre interventional single-blind randomized non-inferiority trial (Treatment)
Trial.Inclusion_Criteria:
Inclusion criteria: 1. Biologically female
2. Aged 18–35 years
3. Insufficiently active based on self-report of not achieving 150 min of moderate to vigorous aerobic physical activity per the Canadian 24-h Movement Guidelines for Adults and deemed generally safe engage in physical activity per completion of the Canadian Society for Exercise Physiology Get Active Questionnaire (GAQ)
Trial.Exclusion_Criteria: Exclusion criteria: Not meeting inclusion criteria
Trial.Condition:
Using different exercise treatments to improve cardiorespiratory fitness in young, insufficiently active but otherwise healthy females.
Other
Trial.Intervention: Briefly, participants will be assigned via block randomization following a 1:1 allocation ratio to either low-volume sprint-interval training (LVSIT) or moderate intensity continuous training (MICT). A randomization sequence will be created using a computerized random number generator (Microsoft Excel). Participants randomized to the LVSIT arm will perform exercise on an electronically braked cycle ergometer (CAROL Bike, Integrated Health Partners, London, UK). Each LVSIT session will involve a 2-min warm-up, 3 × 20-s ‘all-out’ sprints, and a 3-min cooldown. The workload for the sprints will be an individualized resistance determined by a self-learning algorithm that adjusts based on the participants mass, power output, and fatigue index. Participants randomized to the MICT arm will perform exercise on an electronically braked cycle ergometer (Kettler, Ergo Race I, Germany). Each MICT session will involve a 2-min warm-up, 50 min of continuous cycling at a fixed workload that elicits a mean intensity equivalent to ~70% HRmax, and a 3-min cooldown. Training will be performed three times per week for a total of 12 weeks.
Trial.Primary_outcome: Peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak) will be determined by a progressive exercise test to maximal voluntary exertion using an electromagnetically braked cycle ergometer (Lode Excalibur Sport V2.0, Groningen, The Netherlands). Gas exchange and ventilatory variables will be continuously determined using a metabolic cart (Quark CPET metabolic cart, COSMED, Italy). Data will be averaged over 10-s intervals and VO2peak will be defined as the highest 30-s average over three consecutive intervals. VO2peak will be measured in duplicate before and after the 12-week intervention.
Trial.Secondary_outcome:
1. Heart rate measured (Polar A3, Finland) during exercise across all testing and training sessions.
2. Body mass measured using scale before and after the 12-week intervention .
3. Hippocampal-dependent learning and memory measured using the optimized Mnemonic Similarities Task (oMST), before and after the 12-week intervention.
4. Respiratory gases (VCO2, VO2, RER, VE) measured during exercise using metabolic cart (Quark CPET metabolic cart, COSMED, Italy) before and after the 12-week intervention and during select training sessions. Note that post-testing includes two separate trials i.e., at the same absolute and relative intensity as compared to baseline .
5. Serum: BDNF, Plasma: BDNF, cortisol, epinephrine, norepinephrine and insulin measured using commercially available assays, before and after the 12-week intervention . Note that post-testing includes two separate trials i.e., absolute and relative trials to baseline. Blood will be sampled at rest and prior to the cessation of exercise during each submaximal test.
6. [glucose], [pH], [lactate], pCO2, pO2 measured using blood analyzer cards (EPOC; Siemens Healthcare, Ontario, Canada) before and after the 12-week intervention. Note that post-testing includes two separate trials i.e., absolute and relative trials to baseline. Blood will be sampled at rest and prior to the cessation of exercise during each submaximal test.
7. Complete blood count analysis measured by Hamilton Regional Laboratory Medicine Program, Core Laboratory located at McMaster University Medical Centre before and after the 12-week intervention. Note that post-testing includes two separate trials i.e., absolute and relative trials to baseline. Blood will be sampled at rest and prior to the cessation of exercise during each submaximal test.
8. Rating of perceived exertion measured using the Borg Scale, before and after the 12-week intervention, including during training visits.
Trial.Source_Support: Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada
Trial.results_ipd_description: Available on request. The data-sharing plans for the current study are that all data will be made publicly available upon reasonable request from the PI, Dr. Martin Gibala (gibalam@mcmaster.ca).

Trial.Public_title: Use of low oxygen levels in preoperative individuals of Stomach Reduction surgery
Trial.Scientific_title: Effects of Acute Intermittent Hypoxia (AIH) technique in individuals with Obesity in outpatient preoperative preparation for Bariatric Surgery
Trial.Primary_sponsor: Universidade do Estado de Santa Catarina
Trial.Study_design: a phase n/a, randomized-controlled, triple-blind, parallel, prevention
Trial.Contact_Affiliation: Universidade do Estado de Santa Catarina
Trial.Inclusion_Criteria: Inclusion criteria: Obese individuals undergoing preoperative preparation for bariatric surgery, of both sexes, aged between 18 and 60 years, living in Florianópolis and Greater Florianópolis, with no contraindications for physical exercise and agreeing to participate in the study. The adult sample will be obtained intentionally, through accessibility and volunteering.
Trial.Exclusion_Criteria: Exclusion criteria: Participants with a history of malignant and symptomatic arterial hypertension, ischemic heart disease, cancer, uncontrolled metabolic or endocrine disorders or any chronic inflammatory disease, who cannot tolerate the use of a hypoxia exposure mask, with mobility problems, with recent surgery in the last 6 months, surgical complications, psychiatric illnesses, neurological disorders, inability to perform any of the research procedures (lack of understanding or collaboration) and who request their exclusion from the study.
Trial.Intervention: This is a longitudinal, controlled, randomized, triple-blind clinical study. The individuals participating in the training protocol and the pre- and post-training assessments also do not know whether the individual is in the control or experimental group, nor does the statistician know which group the individuals belong to. Randomization will be simple. The experimental group will consist of 10 obese individuals who will inhale a mixture of gases with reduced FIO2 to induce a drop in target oxygen saturation, SpO2. The control group will consist of 10 obese individuals who will receive air in normoxia for the same period of time. For safety reasons, heart rate, target saturation and respiratory rate will be monitored throughout the execution of the protocol. After the hypoxia protocol, both groups will participate in a prehabilitation training for 6 weeks. After the training, the groups will again be subjected to the hypoxia protocol (experimental group) or normoxia (control group).;C23.888.852.079;E02.760.731.850
Trial.Primary_outcome: Investigate the therapeutic effects of the mild Acute Intermittent Hypoxia (AIH) technique on the mean arterial pressure of obese individuals undergoing outpatient preoperative preparation for bariatric surgery; assessed through the use of ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM).
Trial.Secondary_outcome: Investigate the therapeutic influence of mild intermittent acute hypoxia on the functional capacity of obese individuals undergoing outpatient preoperative preparation for bariatric surgery; assessed using the 6-min Walk Test, Time Up and Go Test and 5-repetition Sit-to-Stand Test.;Evaluate the therapeutic influence of acute intermittent hypoxia on respiratory muscle strength in obese individuals undergoing outpatient preoperative preparation for bariatric surgery, assessed through measurements of maximal inspiratory pressure and expiratory pressure.;Observe the therapeutic effects of acute intermittent hypoxia on peripheral muscle strength of obese individuals undergoing outpatient preoperative preparation for bariatric surgery, assessed by measuring quadriceps strength and handgrip strength using dynamometry.;Examine whether mild intermittent acute hypoxia modifies sleep quality and daytime sleepiness in individuals with obesity undergoing outpatient preoperative preparation for bariatric surgery as assessed by the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index.;Determine whether mild intermittent acute hypoxia is capable of modifying the sarcopenia degree, body composition and frailty criteria of individuals with obesity undergoing outpatient preoperative preparation for bariatric surgery, assessed through the application of the SARC-F tool, a questionnaire consisting of five items that assess muscle performance and strength: the individual's difficulty in carrying weight; in lifting, walking and climbing stairs; and occurrence of falls.;Analyze the therapeutic effects of mild intermittent acute hypoxia on the mood state of obese individuals undergoing outpatient preoperative preparation for bariatric surgery, assessed using the Brunel Mood Scale (BRUMS), which measures the mood state of adults and adolescents according to simple mood indicators (feelings of anger, disposition, nervousness and dissatisfaction).;To analyze the influence of acute intermittent hypoxia on heart rate variability and VO2 max estimation of obese individuals undergoing outpatient preoperative preparation for bariatric surgery, assessed through a physical conditioning test and measured using a Polar watch.
Trial.Source_Support: Universidade do Estado de Santa Catarina
Trial.Secondary_Sponsor: Universidade do Estado de Santa Catarina
Trial.results_ipd_description: The data of the unidentified participants will be used for the publication of a scientific article. The protocol, statistical analysis, results found will be disclosed. They will be shared among the researchers of the study to perform statistical analysis and formulation of the same.

Trial.Public_title: Sleep after intensive care study
Trial.Scientific_title: Sedation, memory and sleep disturbances after intensive care: a mixed-methods study
Trial.Primary_sponsor: County Durham and Darlington NHS Foundation Trust
Trial.Study_design: Single-centre mixed-methods observational cross-sectional study (Other, Quality of life, Treatment)
Trial.Inclusion_Criteria:
Inclusion criteria: 1. Aged 18 years or older
2. English-speaking (to ensure language accuracy of data collection)
3. Admitted to ICU for a minimum of 72 hours (to ensure sufficient exposure to the ICU environment relevant to the study aims)
4. No longer requiring critical care (downgraded to ward-level care)
5. Expected to be discharged home within the next 7 days
6. Able to provide informed consent
7. Score negative on a CAM-ICU assessment
8. Score 15/15 on a GCS assessment

For ventilated participants:
9. Must have received continuous sedation for =24 hours during ICU admission
10. Sedation depth must be confirmed by a RASS score of -3 or deeper (as documented in clinical records)
11. Must have been extubated within the ICU setting

For non-sedated participants:
12. Must not have received sedation or ventilation at any point during their hospital admission.

A subset of participants may be invited to take part in a one-off interview. Selection will be based on sleep symptom profiles, although matching across sedation groups may be limited due to timing and sample availability.
Trial.Exclusion_Criteria:
Exclusion criteria: 1. Documented diagnosis of severe cognitive impairment that would affect their ability to participate meaningfully (assessed via clinical records and/or clinician judgement)
2. Currently receiving end-of-life care
3. Non-English speaking
4. Transferring to another hospital
Trial.Condition:
Post-intensive care syndrome (PICS), sleep disturbance, trauma symptoms, memory re-experiencing
Mental and Behavioural Disorders
Trial.Intervention:
Current methodology as of 12/11/2025:
ICU patients will be invited to complete three questionnaires 4 weeks after discharge home. Questionnaires will ask about their ICU memories (ITQ - International Trauma Questionnaire), current sleep experiences (PSQI - Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index) and symptoms of trauma/emotional distress (ICUMT ICU-Memory Types). 10-12 of the participants with high sleep scores will be invited for an hour-long semi-structured interview. Questionnaires and interviews will include both sedated/ventilated and non-sedated/ventilated patient groups. Questionnaire results will be analysed using descriptive statistics and Pearson's correlation; the sedated/no-sedated sub-groups will be compared using t-tests or non-parametric equivalents. Interviews will undergo reflexive thematic analysis to identify patterns in how patients describe their sleep experiences and ICU memories.

Previous methodology:
ICU patients will be invited to complete three questionnaires 2 weeks after discharge home. Questionnaires will ask about their ICU memories (ITQ - International Trauma Questionnaire), current sleep experiences (PSQI - Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index) and symptoms of trauma/emotional distress (ICUMT ICU-Memory Types). 8-10 of the participants with high sleep scores will be invited for an hour-long semi-structured interview and interviews will include both sedated/ventilated and non-sedated/ventilated patient groups. Questionnaire results will be analysed using descriptive statistics and Pearson's correlation; the sedated/no-sedated sub-groups will be compared using t-tests or non-parametric equivalents. Interviews will undergo reflexive thematic analysis to identify patterns in how patients describe their sleep experiences and ICU memories.

Trial.Public_title: How Exercise Improves Muscle Health and Body Composition in Older Adults with Sarcopenia and Sarcopenic Obesity
Trial.Scientific_title: Effects of Exercise Intervention on Sarcopenia Biomarkers and Body Composition in Elderly Men and Women with Sarcopenia and Sarcopenic Obesity
Trial.Study_design: Primary Purpose : Other(This study aims to investigate the effects of exercise intervention on sarcopenia-related biomarkers and body composition in elderly individuals with sarcopenia and sarcop), Intervention Model : Parallel, Blinding/Masking : Open, Allocation : RCT
Trial.Contact_Address: 404, Professor Research Building Gyeongam Gymnasium, 2, Busandaehak-ro 63beon-gil, Geumjeong-gu, Busan 46241, Republic of Korea
Trial.Contact_Affiliation: Pusan National University
Trial.Inclusion_Criteria:
Inclusion criteria: ? Measurement of Body Composition, Sarcopenia, and Sarcopenic Obesity
Body composition will be measured using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA; Lunar Prodigy, GE Medical Systems, Waukesha, WI, USA). Participants will be instructed to abstain from alcohol, diuretics, and caffeine for 48 hours prior to measurement, avoid vigorous physical activity and exercise within 12 hours, and refrain from food and beverage intake for at least 4 hours before the test to minimize measurement errors.

%fat will be calculated as the ratio of fat mass to body weight.

Fat-free mass (FFM) will be obtained by summing the muscle mass of the right and left arms, legs, and trunk.

Appendicular skeletal muscle mass (ASM) will be calculated as the sum of the muscle mass of both arms and legs.

? Criteria for Obesity and Sarcopenia
Obesity will be defined according to Korean standards proposed by Lee (1992), with %fat =30%, rather than the Western criterion of 38% suggested by Baumgartner et al. (2004) and Aubertin-Leheudre et al. (2006).
Sarcopenia will be diagnosed according to the criteria of the Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia in Older People (AWGSOP; Chen et al., 2020):

Muscle strength: Handgrip strength <28 kg for men and <18 kg for women.

Physical performance: Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB) score <9.
If these functional measures are inadequate, body composition will be assessed using DEXA.
Sarcopenia will be further defined using the ASM/m² index (Baumgartner et al., 1998; Newman et al., 2003; Rolland et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2020), with cutoff values of <7.0 kg/m² for men and <5.4 kg/m² for women.

Sarcopenic obesity (SO) will be defined when both the criteria for obesity and sarcopenia are satisfied.
Trial.Exclusion_Criteria:
Exclusion criteria: The exclusion criteria for participant selection in this study are as follows:
? Individuals deemed unable to perform physical activity or exercise based on a physician’s diagnosis.
? Individuals who have participated in an exercise program at least three times per week for more than one month prior to the study.
? Individuals who do not meet the diagnostic criteria for sarcopenia (handgrip strength: <30 kg for men, <20 kg for women; physical performance: SPPB score <8) or obesity (waist circumference: =90 cm for men, =85 cm for women).
Trial.Condition: ;Diseases of the musculoskeletal system and connective tissue
Trial.Intervention:
Others(exercise intervention) : 1. Participant Classification
Elderly individuals will be divided into those with sarcopenia and those with sarcopenic obesity.
Each group will be further stratified by sex (male/female), exercise frequency (3 times/week vs. 5 times/week), and exercise type (aerobic vs. resistance).
Each subgroup will include a control group, resulting in a total of 20 groups (10 sarcopenia + 10 sarcopenic obesity).

2. Exercise Intervention
Duration: 1 year
Frequency: 3 times/week or 5 times/week
Exercise Types:
Aerobic exercise: Low-intensity treadmill walking (30–39% HRR, RPE 9–13)
Resistance exercise: Dumbbell-based exercises including squats, deadlifts, presses, curls, and crunches (Weeks 1–8: 50–59% 1RM; Weeks 9–16: 60–69% 1RM)
Exercise Structure: Warm-up (5–10 min) ? Main exercise (30–40 min) ? Cool-down (5–10 min)

3. Measurements and Assessments

Pre- and Post-tests:
Body composition (DEXA)
Sarcopenia biomarkers (BDNF, Irisin, BMF, FST, Myostatin, GDF-15, TGF-ß, Activins A/B, CLCF-1, fatty acids, etc.)
Muscle strength (handgrip), physical performance (SPPB)
Randomization: Participants will be randomly assigned to intervention or control groups by drawing lots.
Trial.Primary_outcome: Body Composition ;Sarcopenia-related Biomarkers
Trial.Secondary_outcome: Physical Function Muscle strength: Handgrip strength (cut-off: <28 kg for men, <18 kg for women) Physical performance: Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB) score
Trial.results_summary:
1. This study presents the effects of exercise interventions, including variations in type and frequency, on body composition in elderly individuals with sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity, demonstrating their preventive impact on sarcopenia. Furthermore, it investigates both positive and negative sarcopenia-related biomarkers, highlighting potential positive biomarkers.
2. hrough this project, it was found that while lean body mass (LBM) did not change significantly, percent body fat (%fat) showed significant reductions in both the aerobic exercise group (5 sessions/week) and the resistance exercise group (5 sessions/week).
3. Among the positive biomarkers (Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor, Irisin) and negative biomarkers (Growth Differentiation Factor-8, Growth Differentiation Factor-15), significant improvements were observed in BDNF and Irisin, specifically in the aerobic exercise group (5 sessions/week) and the resistance exercise group (5 sessions/week), respectively.
4. These findings suggest that optimal exercise prescriptions for elderly individuals with sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity require regular participation in aerobic and resistance exercise five times per week.
5. The outcomes of this project will be disseminated as research publications and patent applications, and follow-up longitudinal studies in populations with sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity will be pursued in the future.
Trial.results_ipd_description: Available on Request : onlylove8383@pusan.ac.kr

Trial.Scientific_title: Effect of Physical Training and Hypocaloric Diet on ventilatory efficiency during progressive exercise in patients with Metabolic Syndrome
Trial.Study_design: a phase n/a, single-arm-study, open, single-group, treatment
Trial.Contact_Affiliation: Universidade Federal de São Paulo
Trial.Inclusion_Criteria: Inclusion criteria: Sedentary women; between 18 and 50 years old; with Metabolic Syndrome, according to the National Cholesterol Education Program, Adult Treatment Panel III criteria.
Trial.Exclusion_Criteria: Exclusion criteria: Women enrolled in other physical training programs; undergoing dietary treatment; smokers; with a history of alcohol consumption; with cardiovascular disease or a metabolic condition beyond those already included in Metabolic Syndrome; with less than 75% participation in physical training sessions; who experience changes in medication during the experimental protocol.
Trial.Intervention: 43 adult women, aged 18 to 50, diagnosed with Metabolic Syndrome according to the National Cholesterol Education Program, Adult Treatment Panel III (NCEP, ATP-III) criteria, will be evaluated. Volunteers who agree to participate and fit the sample criteria will undergo a medical evaluation and complete all initial examinations: three blood pressure measurements, body weight assessment, body mass index (BMI), waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio, laboratory tests (serum levels of total cholesterol, triglycerides, HDL-cholesterol, and glycemia), and a cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET). Subsequently, they will be referred for dietary and physical training intervention. All patients will undergo 4 months of intervention and repeat all assessments. Patients will be guided and monitored bi-weekly by a nutritionist in following a hypocaloric, low-glycemic index diet, reduced by 500 kilocalories, with the goal of losing at least two kilograms per month. Physical training will be performed 3 times per week. The training prescription will be individualized, with sessions lasting approximately 60 minutes, comprising 5 minutes of warm-up, 45 minutes of aerobic exercise (treadmill or exercise bike), 10 minutes of localized muscle resistance exercises, and 5 minutes of relaxation, totaling 60 minutes of physical exercise. The intensity of the first 10 sessions will be at the anaerobic threshold (AT), in the next 10 sessions the intensity will be between the AT and the respiratory compensation point (RCP), and in the last 32 sessions the intensity will be close to the RCP, with intensity controlled by heart rate obtained from the CPET. At the end of the 4-month intervention period, all assessments will be performed again.;I02.233.543;E02.642.249.200

Trial.Public_title: Psychological Effects of Character Strengths Interventions According to School Adjustment Levels
Trial.Scientific_title: The moderating role of school adjustment on the effects of strength-based interventions on subjective and psychological wellbeing
Trial.Study_design: Primary Purpose : Other(An educational intervention study to promote wellbeing and school adjustment among elementary school students), Intervention Model : Parallel, Blinding/Masking : Open, Allocation : Non-RCT
Trial.Contact_Affiliation: Seoul National University
Trial.Inclusion_Criteria:
Inclusion criteria: Fifth- and sixth-grade elementary school students enrolled in schools in metropolitan areas
Students whose parents or legal guardians provided written informed consent
Students who personally assented to participate in the study
Students able to take part in classroom activities and complete brief questionnaire
Trial.Exclusion_Criteria:
Exclusion criteria: Students without written parental (legal guardian) consent or personal assent
Students who failed attention-check items during assessments (e.g., inconsistent or patterned responses)
Students who withdrew from the study or provided incomplete data that could not be analyzed
Trial.Intervention: Others(Educational program (character strengths interventions and emotion-focused program)) : This study compared four conditions among fifth- and sixth-grade elementary students. (1) Signature strengths group: identifying and applying one’s top strengths for one week; (2) Growth strengths group: identifying and developing less-used strengths; (3) Combined group: integrating both signature and growth strengths activities; (4) Active control group: creating an “emotion dictionary” and observing emotions. Each program included one 80-minute classroom session and seven days of structured daily practice.
Trial.Primary_outcome: Basic Psychological Needs Satisfaction (autonomy, competence, relatedness)
Trial.Secondary_outcome: Subjective wellbeing (happiness)
Trial.results_summary: This study examined 533 fifth- and sixth-grade students who participated in character strengths interventions (signature, growth, combined) or an emotion-focused active control condition. Overall, the interventions did not show clear advantages over the active control. However, among students with low levels of school adjustment, participation in the growth-strengths intervention led to significant improvements in autonomy and competence. No notable effects were found for relatedness or subjective wellbeing. These findings suggest that focusing on the development of under-expressed “growth strengths” may be particularly beneficial for students struggling with school adjustment.

Trial.Public_title: Exercises to improve Back Pain in elderly people treated in public health services
Trial.Scientific_title: Effectiveness of an Exercise Program for elderly people with Chronic Low Back Pain treated in Primary Health Care
Trial.Primary_sponsor: Universidade Federal de Juiz de Fora - UFJF
Trial.Study_design: a phase n/a, randomized-controlled, open, parallel, treatment
Trial.Contact_Affiliation: Universidade Federal de Juiz de Fora (UFJF)
Trial.Inclusion_Criteria: Inclusion criteria: Aged 60 years or older; both sexes; report chronic low back pain, defined as the presence of symptoms in the lumbar region for a period longer than three months; present a score of four or higher on the Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire and pain intensity greater than three on the Visual Analog Scale (VAS)
Trial.Exclusion_Criteria: Exclusion criteria: Individuals presenting with radiculopathies; severe spinal pathologies such as cauda equina syndrome, fractures, or cancer; history of spinal surgery within the past 12 months; signs of cognitive impairment; pregnancy; or absolute and relative contraindications to exercise, as described in the guidelines of the American College of Sports Medicine
Trial.Intervention: This is a longitudinal, experimental study, designed as an open-label, randomized controlled clinical trial with two arms. The experimental group will consist of 60 older adults of both sexes with chronic low back pain who will receive a group exercise program as treatment in Primary Health Care. Sessions will take place three times a week, each lasting 60 minutes, over a period of eight weeks. The control group will consist of 60 older adults of both sexes with chronic low back pain who will receive a placebo intervention, consisting of the application of an elastic tape measuring 5 centimeters in width and 5 millimeters in thickness on the lower back, with the initial anchor point located at the region of the first sacral vertebra (0 percent tension). After the application, the participant will be instructed to return to normal activities and to keep the tape on for 72 hours. If the participant develops any type of skin reaction, they will be instructed to remove the tape immediately. The tape will be replaced every three days, as recommended by previous studies. To ensure random allocation of the sample in both the feasibility study and the randomized controlled trial, participants will be randomized into two groups using opaque, sealed, and sequentially numbered envelopes. The randomization process will be conducted using the RAND function of Microsoft Office Excel. The researcher responsible for data analysis and the evaluator will remain blinded to the participants’ group allocation. To ensure confidentiality, data will be coded anonymously, without any information that could identify the individual's randomization;E02.760.169.063.500.387;E02.760.169.063.500;N04.590.233.727

;Expected Outcome 3: A self-reported clinical improvement is expected to be observed in the three- and six-month follow-up assessments, as measured by the Global Perceived Effect (GPE) Scale.
